name: Franciscan Church, Ferenciek tere
address: Ferenciek tere 9, 1053 Budapest (corner of Kossuth Lajos utca 1)
intro: The Franciscan church stands on the corner of Ferenciek tere and Kossuth Lajos utca in Pest's Inner City. Its main front is Baroque, built in the early eighteenth century, while the tower beside the nave is a Romantic addition of the mid-nineteenth century. The church gave the square its name, and a relief recalling the 1838 flood is set into its wall.
about: The Alcantarai Szent Péter-templom, usually called the Franciscan church (ferences templom), is the Roman Catholic church of the Franciscan friars in the Inner City. It is a protected monument, registered under the addresses Ferenciek tere 9 and Kossuth Lajos utca 1, and it is the church that gave Ferenciek tere its name, which means Franciscans’ Square.

The heritage register describes a three-bay Baroque main facade without a tower, with Doric pilasters, a three-part cornice and a curved central gable. Above the main portal stands the Virgin Mary on a globe, holding the Christ Child, with winged angels at her sides. Below it is a relief with a scene from the Way of the Cross, and above it is the Franciscan coat of arms. Statues of saints, among them Francis of Assisi, Anthony of Padua and Peter of Alcántara, complete the front.

The tower rises on the south side, next to the nave and chancel, joined to the former friary building, which the register says is today the Ferences bazaar. Its octagonal spire has oval windows and obelisks at the corners. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that the interior’s acoustics and its organ make the church suitable for classical concerts.

On the side wall facing Kossuth Lajos utca, a bronze relief honours Baron Miklós Wesselényi and the flood of 1838. The register’s list of nearby objects places the Néreidák fountain, the Párisi Udvar and the Megyeháza within about 100 metres, so the church is surrounded by other historic Inner City buildings.
tips: This is a working parish church of the Franciscans. Dress and behave as in any place of worship, keep your voice low and avoid photographing during services; ask the parish about visiting arrangements before you plan a stop.
Walk round to the Kossuth Lajos utca side to find the Wesselényi flood relief, which is set into the wall on the Kossuth Lajos utca side.
The Baroque front and the Romantic tower are easiest to appreciate together from a little distance across the square; a wide lens helps in a crowded street.
Do not confuse it with the Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption, which has its own page. The Párisi Udvar and the Néreidák fountain are nearby.

history.intro: The surviving building is mainly the work of two periods, the Baroque rebuilding of the early 1700s and the Romantic tower of the 1850s and 1860s, but the Franciscans’ presence here goes back much further.

sections.heading: Medieval friars and the Ottoman years
paragraphs: A Budapest city-history article says the Franciscans built a Gothic chapel and friary dedicated to St Peter between about 1250 and 1260 and began converting it into a church late in the thirteenth century. The same article says that after the Ottomans arrived in 1541 the building served as a mosque until they were driven out, and that the Franciscans were given it back in the early 1700s.

Hungarian Wikipedia gives a different account of the earliest period: it dates the first church to after the Mongol invasion of 1241, attributes it to King Béla IV, and says the friars returned in the 1690s. Hungarian Wikipedia also says the church was not destroyed under Ottoman rule but was out of use from the 1500s, which is not the same as becoming a mosque. The sources therefore agree on the medieval Franciscan origin but not on the details, and the early dates should be read as approximate.

sections.heading: Baroque church, Romantic tower
paragraphs: The heritage register gives 1717–1743 as the Baroque construction period and names Ferenc Wieser as the architect of the Baroque church. Hungarian Wikipedia gives 1743 as the year of reconsecration but does not name a designer. The Romantic tower and spire were added between 1858 and 1863.

The square took its name from the church. According to the city-history article, the area in front of the church was called Barát tér, meaning Friars’ Square, from 1727, and Ferenciek tere was made an official name in 1874. The neighbouring Kígyó tér was renamed Apponyi tér in 1921 and Felszabadulás tér in 1953; in 1991 it and the area in front of the church were joined under the name Ferenciek tere.

sections.heading: Flood, grave and nationalisation
paragraphs: The 1838 flood reached the building. Holló Barnabás created the bronze relief of Baron Miklós Wesselényi in 1900, and it was installed on the church wall in 1905. Hungarian Wikipedia also records that the crypt held the first grave of the executed prime minister Lajos Batthyány until 1870.

During the nationalisation of the communist period the Franciscans had to leave the church and friary, and they returned in 1990. The tower holds four bells, all cast by László Szlezák in 1928; the largest weighs 2,967 kg.

name: University Church (Church of the Virgin Mary's Nativity)
intro: The University Church, or Egyetemi templom, is a twin-towered Baroque church beside Egyetem tér in Pest's Inner City, dedicated to the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. The Pauline order built it in the eighteenth century, and it has served the university since 1786. A restoration that began in 2019 was reported finished in September 2020.
about: The Egyetemi templom, also called the Kisboldogasszony-templom, is a Roman Catholic church on Papnövelde utca, by Egyetem tér. It belongs to the Budapest-Belváros parish and is run by a church directorate whose director is the rector of the neighbouring Central Seminary. The archdiocese calls it one of the most beautiful late Baroque churches in the country, thanks to its Pauline carved furnishings.

The heritage register describes a two-towered Baroque front with composite pilasters on the lower two levels and Corinthian pilasters above. The pediment between the towers holds a radiant Eye of God and statues of Saints Paul the Hermit and Anthony the Hermit, shown with a lion, a palm tree and a raven. The carved wooden doors have a curved broken pediment above them, and a statue of the Immaculate Conception stands in a niche on the central axis. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the height of each tower as 56 metres.

Inside, the single nave is covered by a Bohemian cap vault with chapels on both sides, and in the middle of the nineteenth century the walls were covered with imitation marble. The high altar by Antal Lipót Conti depicts the Birth of Mary and is flanked by statues of the two hermit saints by József Hebenstreit. The archdiocese dates the frescoes to 1776 and attributes them to Johann Bergl and his students.

The church stands between university buildings: the register mentions the Faculty of Law and the Academy of Theology on either side. Its mission has been pastoral care for students and, especially after 1900, for the city’s intellectuals. The church also has an urn cemetery, which the archdiocese states is not accessible to the public.
tips: Treat it as a place of worship: dress modestly, keep your voice low and do not photograph during services. The archdiocese’s page is the place to check for current visiting arrangements.
The archdiocese states that the church’s urn cemetery is not accessible to the public, so do not look for a way in.
Stand back on the square or in the street to see both towers and the pediment sculpture in one frame.
Do not confuse it with the Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption, which has its own page, or with other churches nearby. The Hungarian National Museum is within a short walk.

history.intro: The church replaced a mosque and took the Pauline order several decades to complete, from the purchase of the plot in 1688 to the finishing of the second tower in 1771.

sections.heading: The Paulines build on a former mosque site
paragraphs: According to the archdiocese, the Pauline order bought the plot in 1688; it held a mosque and a few houses. Work on the monastery began in 1715, and in 1720 the mosque was demolished and a chapel built with funds from Mária Magdolna Doloczky. The archdiocese gives 8 April 1725 for the laying of the foundation stone, while Hungarian Wikipedia gives 1723.

Sources differ over who designed it. The heritage register names András Mayerhoffer as architect and dates the construction to 1722–1742, while Hungarian Wikipedia says he was probably the architect. A 2020 news report lists Mátyás Drenker, Mayerhoffer and then master Márton Siegl as leading the work.

sections.heading: Consecration, towers and a university church
paragraphs: Archbishop Gábor Patachich of Kalocsa celebrated the first Mass on 8 September 1742 and consecrated the church the following day. The main gate, pews, pulpit and choir screen followed between 1744 and 1748, with the high altar in 1746. The towers were finished in 1768 and 1771, according to the archdiocese; Hungarian Wikipedia says the exterior was completed only in 1770.

In 1786 the Pauline order was dissolved and the church became the church of Pázmány Péter University. From 1803 it was shared with the Central Seminary, housed in the former monastery. After the Second World War it was restored under the Budapest Monument Protection Authority, and in 1950 it became the Belvárosi Kisboldogasszony church administration.

sections.heading: Preachers, an early photograph and restoration
paragraphs: The archdiocese names Ottokár Prohászka, Tihamér Tóth, Sándor Sík and Ferenc Gál among the well-known preachers of its pulpit. Hungarian Wikipedia notes that a daguerreotype from around 1844, taken of Kecskeméti utca from the Kálvin tér side, shows the church’s towers and is described as the oldest surviving photograph of Pest.

A restoration began in May 2019 with state support. It covered cleaning and repair of the tower’s copper cladding, restoration of the sculptures, the sacristy, new floor covering and updated heating and electrics. News reports in September 2020 describe the church as renovated.

name: Servite Church (Inner City St Anne's Church)
intro: The Servite Church, officially the Inner City St Anne’s Church, stands on Szervita tér in Pest. The Servite order built it between 1725 and 1732, and its late Baroque interior is described as one of the most richly gilded in Budapest. It is a different church from St Anne’s on Batthyány tér in Buda.
about: The Belvárosi Szent Anna-templom, known to most people as the Servite church (szervita templom), is a Roman Catholic church at Szervita tér 6, in the Belváros-Nagyboldogasszony parish. Its patron is St Anne. The parish calls it a quiet Baroque church in central Budapest and notes that its proportions give it excellent acoustics.

The interior is the reason to look inside. According to the parish, the pulpit carries gilded figures of the four Evangelists, the main altarpiece shows St Anne with the child Mary and St Joachim, and gilded wooden statues of St Stephen, St Ladislaus, St John the Baptist and St Joseph stand beside the high altar. A fresco above the organ loft shows St Stephen offering the Holy Crown to the Virgin Mary. A painting of the seven Servite founders hangs on the right side of the nave and a large painting of the Archangel Raphael with the young Tobias on the left.

The heritage register describes a detached, single-nave church with one tower and later eclectic alterations. The three-bay main facade has Corinthian pilasters and a segmental pediment, the square tower has Ionic corner pilasters, a balustrade and a lantern, and saint statues stand in niches on the first floor. At the entrance a relief by János Istók of 1930 commemorates the First World War.

Only the church survives from the original Servite complex. The register notes that it is partly enclosed by a modern building complex, so it is seen among newer buildings. The parish says pilgrims came for nearly three centuries to the feasts of St Anne on 26 July and of Our Lady of Sorrows on 15 September.
tips: The parish website lists visiting arrangements, including for the crypt. These change, so check the official page before you go rather than relying on a printed guide.
Make sure you have the right church: this is the Pest-side Servite church on Szervita tér, not St Anne’s Church on Batthyány tér in Buda, which has its own page.
It is a working church, so keep your voice low, dress modestly and photograph the gilded interior without disturbing services or worshippers.
Vörösmarty tér and the Deák Ferenc tér Lutheran church are a short walk away, which makes it easy to combine with a walk through downtown Pest.

history.intro: The Servite church has been rebuilt, damaged and surrounded by new buildings more than once. Its Baroque core dates from the 1720s, while the monastery beside it did not survive the twentieth century.

sections.heading: A Servite church on a mosque site
paragraphs: The parish says that in 1686, after Pest was freed from Ottoman rule, the Servite order received permission to build a church and friary on the site of a former mosque, and that the church was built between 1725 and 1732. Hungarian Wikipedia puts the order’s settlement in 1689 and the start of work on the church in 1717, with the monastery begun in 1725 and the church finished by 1732.

Hungarian Wikipedia names János Hölbling as the original designer, who died before the work was finished, and János György Pauer as the construction supervisor who completed the church by 1732. The register describes the building as Baroque with later eclectic alterations.

sections.heading: Bombardment and a new facade
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia reports that the church and monastery were badly damaged in May 1849 during Heinrich Hentzi’s artillery bombardment of Pest. The parish records that the facade was remodelled in 1871, when the tower was raised by one storey, and the heritage register notes saint statues on the first floor by László Halász from 1873.
The same Hungarian Wikipedia entry says József Diescher rebuilt the monastery in 1871–1874 so that its facade matched the church’s.

sections.heading: War damage and the surviving church
paragraphs: The parish says the Servite order was dissolved in 1948 and that its priests went on serving at the church until 1960; Hungarian Wikipedia says the order ran the church until the end of the Second World War. In the winter of 1944 a bomb hit the monastery and the attached apartment building, and much of the complex collapsed. The ruins were never restored and were demolished in 1964.

A large modern building was later put up on the monastery site and crowded the church. The parish calls it a post office and Hungarian Wikipedia a telephone exchange. It was replaced by a hotel and residential complex, which the parish dates to 2020 and Hungarian Wikipedia to 2018. The parish records that the facade, renovated with city, archdiocesan and district funding, was blessed by Cardinal Péter Erdő on 21 December 2014.

name: Kálvin tér Reformed Church
intro: The Kálvin tér Reformed Church is a neoclassical church beside Kálvin tér in district IX (Ferencváros), next to the Inner City. Built between 1816 and 1830 and protected as a monument, it is described as the largest Reformed church in Budapest. A columned portico, a single tower and a cross-shaped interior define the building.
about: The Kálvin téri református templom is the church of the Budapest-Kálvin Tér Reformed congregation, at Kálvin tér 7. The congregation says it was founded in 1796 and calls itself one of the oldest and most important Protestant congregations in Pest. The church has stood on the square since 1830 and is described on the parish site as neoclassical.

The heritage register describes a rectangular building with a single tower above the entrance, topped by a tall onion dome and a star-shaped finial. A portico of four Corinthian columns carries a triangular pediment, and the doors bear an inscription carved on a stone book that reads ‘AZ IGAZ ISTENNEK’, roughly ‘to the true God’. On the north-western wall stand a bronze bust of László Ravasz, a former pastor and bishop who served here, and a red limestone wall fountain.

Inside, the plan is cross-shaped, with a flat central dome, barrel-vaulted arms, a gallery for the organ and two-storey side galleries. The pulpit sits beneath a half-dome, and a U-shaped crypt lies below the building. Hungarian Wikipedia says the windows of the attached Kálvin Hall hold stained glass by Miksa Róth showing John Calvin, István Bocskai and Gábor Bethlen; the sources used here do not say whether visitors can see them, so do not plan a visit around the glass.

The parish site is aimed at a living congregation, with services, choirs, youth and student groups and charity work. It mentions tourists only in passing, among the people who come to the square, and describes no tours of the building, so visitors should treat the church as a working place of worship and ask the parish about access. The church is in district IX (Ferencváros), beside the Inner City.
tips: The parish site gives no visiting arrangements for tourists, so contact the parish or check its page before planning to go inside, and respect services and other congregational activities.
Dress and behave as in any church; photograph the interior only where it is clearly acceptable.
The portico and tower are best seen from the square; the wall fountain and the Ravasz bust are on the north-western wall.
The Hungarian National Museum and the Great Market Hall are both within an easy walk, and the Deák Ferenc tér Lutheran church makes an interesting comparison.

history.intro: The congregation is older than its building: it dates its founding to 1796, while the present church was built over fourteen years from 1816 and then changed by later additions and renovations.

sections.heading: Designing and building the church, 1816–1830
paragraphs: The heritage register gives 1816–1830 as the construction period for the classicist church and names József Hofrichter as its designer. Hungarian Wikipedia credits Vince Hild with the original plans, so sources differ on who drew them. The register also records later work by József Hild on the building.
Hungarian Wikipedia adds that two towers were originally planned and the foundations for both were laid, but only one tower was built, resting on the inner edges of those foundations.

sections.heading: Portico, galleries and tomb
paragraphs: According to the register, József Hild designed the pulpit canopy in 1831, the portico in 1848 and the gallery in 1854; the organ is by the Deutschmann firm. Hungarian Wikipedia says the side galleries were paid for by a bequest from Countess Sarolta Strachan, and that the tower reached its present form with the spire in 1859.

The register records the tomb of Zichy Manóné from 1854, attributed to Raymond Gaiard and Frigyes Feszl. Hungarian Wikipedia says the countess’s ashes lie in the crypt, in a Gothic Revival setting by Feszl, with a sarcophagus by the French sculptor Raymond Gayrard.

sections.heading: Bells, metro works and renovation
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the original large bell was cast in 1833 by Henrik Eberhardt and rang at noon on Petőfi Rádió from 1933 to 2006. It cracked in 1980, and a new bell was cast the same year by Lajos Gombos, weighing 1050 kg and reusing the old bronze. Two smaller bells requisitioned in the First World War were never replaced.
A full renovation took place in 2013–2014, linked to the construction of Metro Line 4, during which the tower was reinforced with steel.

name: György Ráth Villa (Museum of Applied Arts)
intro: The György Ráth Villa on Városligeti fasor in Terézváros was built in 1880 and later housed the collection of György Ráth, the first director-general of the Museum of Applied Arts. Since autumn 2018 it has shown the permanent exhibition ‘Our Art Nouveau’, drawn from that museum’s own collection.
about: The Ráth György-villa is one of the sites of the Museum of Applied Arts (Iparművészeti Múzeum), standing at Városligeti fasor 12 in the sixth district. Its permanent exhibition, A mi szecessziónk (‘Our Art Nouveau’), presents highlights of the museum’s Art Nouveau collection. Hungarian Wikipedia says it contains nearly 600 objects.

According to the same entry, the display covers British, Austrian and French Art Nouveau, with Zsolnay ceramics, Gallé and Tiffany glass and Lalique jewellery. Bugatti furniture reflects Eastern influence, and two contemporary glass artists are also represented. So the show works both as an introduction to the style and as a look at the museum’s holdings.

The building is itself part of the story. According to the museum, the architect Géza Györgyi remodelled the villa; the metal staircase railing is by Gyula Jungfer, and the staircase and hall furniture were made to ideas by Pál Horti. Hungarian Wikipedia calls the villa an eclectic building from 1880.

The villa stands on Városligeti fasor, an avenue named after the City Park (Városliget), near Andrássy út and the Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts, which ran this villa as the China Museum from 1954. The museum states that the villa is not wheelchair accessible because of its heritage protection and architecture. It also says the exhibition makes the collection available during the reconstruction of the main building; check the museum’s page for the current state of both.
tips: Check the Museum of Applied Arts’ page for the villa before you go: it covers current visiting arrangements, capacity and accessibility, and the museum ties the villa exhibition to the reconstruction of its main building on Üllői út, so look at the museum’s site for that building’s current status.
The museum states that the building is not wheelchair accessible, for heritage and architectural reasons, so plan accordingly.
Pair it with the Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts, which ran this villa as the China Museum, or with a walk along Andrássy út to the City Park.
Look at the staircase and entrance hall as well as the display cases; the railing and furniture are part of the Art Nouveau story.

history.intro: The house was built in 1880, became a collector’s home and museum in the early twentieth century, spent decades as an East Asian art museum and reopened as an Art Nouveau showcase in 2018.

sections.heading: A collector’s villa and the Ráth Museum
paragraphs: György Ráth (1828–1905) was the first director-general of the Museum of Applied Arts and a major private collector of his day. He bought the villa in 1901 and, together with his wife Gizella Melcsiczky, filled it with art objects.

After his death his widow donated the collection to the Museum of Applied Arts on condition that it be kept together as a public museum named after him. The Ráth György Museum was presented to the press at a ceremony in November 1906, and Emperor Franz Joseph visited it on 8 January 1907.

sections.heading: The China Museum years and closure
paragraphs: After the Second World War the museum’s independence and collections were dismantled under the communist regime. In 1954 the building was handed to the Ferenc Hopp Museum of East Asian Art and renamed the China Museum, and many original objects were transferred to other national museums.

After the political changes of the early 1990s the building regained its original name and hosted East Asian exhibitions until it closed in 2014. Only a memorial room in the reconstructed dining room recalled Ráth.

sections.heading: Reopening as ‘Our Art Nouveau’
paragraphs: The villa reopened in autumn 2018 with the permanent exhibition A mi szecessziónk. Hungarian Wikipedia gives 14 September 2018 as the date and says the exhibition also marked 190 years since Ráth’s birth.

The museum’s page links the reopening to the reconstruction of its main building. It does not give a date for that building’s return, so visitors should look at the official page for the current status.
